prompt.context: Jeff Zucker, the CEO of NBC has asked you for help. In 2006 NBC had profits of $3B on revenue of $16.5B; these numbers have fallen 10% over the past three quarters. There has been an $8M drop in ad-revenue due to the proliferation of specialized cable channels as well as changing viewer preferences in media consumption. NBC's goals include achieving double-digit growth, reducing costs by $750M, and spending $150M in digital initiatives in order to grow $400M in revenue (from digital delivery) to $1B. Programming costs for television shows have risen as shows average 60 scenes (vs. 40 scenes previously). Big-budget shows such as Heroes cost $2.5M/episode and charge $200K/spot (there are 20 spots/hr). In addition, on-demand media has cut into revenues although live entertainment is still a draw.
prompt.question: What are your initial thoughts about NBC's troubles? Should NBC redirect resources towards low-budget shows? How should NBC use the $150M set aside for digital initiatives?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other revenue streams affected beyond advertising?
clarifying_info.a: Concede that syndication, DVD sales, and other revenue streams are relevant considerations.

clarifying_info.q: Will advertisers pay less for low-budget show demographics?
clarifying_info.a: That's already reflected in the price — focus on other angles.

clarifying_info.q: Do low-budget shows also air 20 spots per hour?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume 20 spots/hr for low-budget shows as well.

framework: Diagnose profitability decline: revenue decline (ad revenue drop, viewer fragmentation, on-demand cannibalization) vs. cost increases (more scenes per show, rising programming costs)
Quantify the low-budget show trade-off: compare per-episode profit of big-budget vs. low-budget programming
Assess non-advertising revenue implications: syndication rights, DVD sales, streaming licensing — low-budget shows may have lower value in these channels
Evaluate digital initiatives: how to allocate $150M to generate $400M incremental digital revenue toward the $1B digital target
Strategic fit: does a shift to low-budget programming align with NBC's brand and long-term competitive position?

questions.prompt: What are your initial thoughts about NBC's troubles?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify both the revenue and cost sides: ad revenue erosion from cable fragmentation and changing consumption habits (on-demand, digital); rising programming costs (60 scenes vs. 40 scenes, higher per-episode budgets). Candidates should note NBC's stated goals — double-digit growth, $750M cost reduction, and $1B digital revenue — as the framework for prioritization. This is a qualitative synthesis question delivered rapid-fire; candidates should structure their answer clearly without needing a pause.

questions.prompt: If a low-budget show like Deal or No Deal costs $1M per episode, how much less revenue per spot can NBC afford to charge and still retain the profitability of big-budget shows?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate big-budget profit per episode, then back-solve for the minimum per-spot price that generates the same profit on a low-budget show.

math.setup: Big-budget: cost = $2.5M/episode, revenue = $200K/spot × 20 spots = $4M/episode, profit = $4M − $2.5M = $1.5M. Low-budget: cost = $1M/episode, must achieve same profit of $1.5M, so required revenue = $1M + $1.5M = $2.5M. With 20 spots/hr: price per spot = $2.5M ÷ 20.
steps: Max price per spot for low-budget: $2.5M ÷ 20 = $125K
math.answer: NBC can charge as low as $125K/spot on a low-budget show and still match big-budget show profitability — i.e., it can afford a $75K/spot reduction.

questions.prompt: Given this info, should Zucker redirect resources towards low-budget shows? What else should he consider?
questions.guidance: The 'answer' is NOT simply 'yes, lower costs = same profit.' A strong candidate explores revenue streams beyond advertising: (1) Syndication rights — big-budget prestige dramas command higher syndication fees than game shows; (2) DVD/home video sales — scripted dramas sell; game shows typically do not; (3) international licensing; (4) brand perception and advertiser premiums tied to quality programming; (5) long-run audience loyalty. The interviewer should stonewall any answer that focuses only on ad revenue (e.g., 'advertisers will like the demographic less') and concede answers about long-term strategy, competition, and non-advertising revenue.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm how to best use the $150M set aside for digital initiatives.
questions.guidance: This tests awareness of digital media trends circa 2006–2007. Strong answers cover multiple categories: streaming/on-demand platforms (invest in NBC.com or partner with emerging platforms), digital content distribution (repurpose existing content for web/mobile), original digital-first content, data and personalization to improve ad targeting, interactive advertising formats, and partnerships with technology companies. Candidates should acknowledge that the goal is to grow digital revenue from an implied base to $1B (a $400M incremental increase from an unspecified base, with $150M invested).

brainstorming.prompt: How should NBC allocate the $150M in digital initiatives to maximize digital revenue growth toward the $1B target?

categories.name: Streaming & On-Demand Platforms
ideas: Build out NBC.com with full-episode streaming
Partner with or invest in emerging streaming services

categories.name: Digital Content Distribution
ideas: Distribute content via iTunes, YouTube, and mobile carriers

categories.name: Original Digital Content
ideas: Fund web-original series at lower cost
Create companion digital content for TV shows

categories.name: Technology & Infrastructure
ideas: Invest in DRM and anti-piracy technology

recommendation: Do not redirect resources entirely to low-budget programming — the math shows equivalent episodic ad profit, but non-advertising revenues (syndication, DVD, international licensing) favor scripted big-budget content
Use digital initiatives ($150M) to build streaming and on-demand infrastructure that monetizes the existing content library and reduces cannibalization by on-demand platforms
Pursue selective cost reduction by mixing low-budget formats (game shows, reality) into the schedule to hit the $750M cost target without abandoning prestige scripted programming
risks: Brand erosion if NBC becomes associated primarily with low-budget game shows
Syndication and DVD revenue decline if scripted pipeline is cut
Digital investment may take several years to reach the $1B revenue target
next_steps: Quantify syndication and DVD revenue by show type to confirm the full P&L impact of a programming mix shift
Model digital revenue scenarios under different investment allocations
Benchmark competitor (ABC, CBS, Fox) programming mix and digital strategies
